raw_text:
Angiotensin receptor–neprilysin inhibition (ARNI) with sacubitril/valsartan couples blockade of the angiotensin II type 1 receptor with neprilysin inhibition, thereby suppressing maladaptive renin–angiotensin–aldosterone signaling while augmenting natriuretic peptide, bradykinin, adrenomedullin, and cyclic guanosine monophosphate pathways [1]. This dual mechanism provides vasodilatory, natriuretic, antifibrotic, and antihypertrophic effects, but also explains practical safety issues: hypotension is more frequent than with angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors (ACEIs), whereas cough, hyperkalemia, and renal dysfunction are generally not increased and may be reduced.

The pivotal evidence in heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF) is PARADIGM-HF, in which sacubitril/valsartan was superior to enalapril in 8442 ambulatory symptomatic patients, reducing cardiovascular death or first heart-failure hospitalization, cardiovascular death, first heart-failure hospitalization, and all-cause mortality [2]. Subsequent analyses strengthened the interpretation that ARNI modifies disease trajectory rather than simply delaying a first event: it reduced clinical progression among survivors [3], 30-day readmission after heart-failure hospitalization [4], and recurrent heart-failure admissions [5]. Patient-centered benefits were also evident, with modest but consistent improvements or less deterioration in Kansas City Cardiomyopathy Questionnaire scores [6]. Benefits were preserved across clinically relevant groups, including older patients [7] and patients with diabetes, in whom glycemic indices improved relative to enalapril [8].

Mechanistic and remodeling studies support the clinical signal. In EVALUATE-HF, sacubitril/valsartan did not significantly improve the primary aortic stiffness measure versus enalapril at 12 weeks but improved several echocardiographic remodeling indices [9]. In PROVE-HF, reductions in NT-proBNP after ARNI initiation correlated with improvements in left ventricular volumes, ejection fraction, left atrial volume, and diastolic parameters, suggesting reverse remodeling [10]. Health status also improved after initiation in PROVE-HF [11], and pooled PROVE-HF/EVALUATE-HF analyses clarified that early BNP rises can occur because neprilysin degrades BNP, whereas NT-proBNP remains the preferred biomarker for monitoring response [12].

Hospitalization is now recognized as an opportunity to start disease-modifying therapy. PIONEER-HF enrolled stabilized patients hospitalized for acute decompensated HFrEF and showed greater early NT-proBNP reduction with sacubitril/valsartan than enalapril, without excess renal dysfunction, hyperkalemia, symptomatic hypotension, or angioedema [13]. Benefits and tolerability were maintained across achieved dose levels [14], and open-label extension data supported in-hospital rather than delayed post-discharge initiation [15]. TRANSITION showed that starting sacubitril/valsartan before discharge or shortly after discharge was feasible in stabilized patients [16]. TITRATION provided practical support for gradual uptitration, particularly in patients with lower previous ACEI/ARB exposure or lower blood pressure [17]. In contrast, LIFE, enrolling advanced HFrEF with recent class IV symptoms, did not show superiority over valsartan for NT-proBNP and highlighted higher rates of treatment discontinuation, emphasizing that frail, hypotensive, or end-stage patients may derive less tolerable benefit [18].

The evidence is more nuanced in heart failure with mildly reduced or preserved ejection fraction (HFmrEF/HFpEF). PARAMOUNT, a phase 2 HFpEF trial, showed greater NT-proBNP reduction and favorable left atrial remodeling versus valsartan [19]. PARAGON-HF narrowly missed statistical significance for its primary composite of total heart-failure hospitalizations and cardiovascular death, but suggested greater benefit in patients with lower ejection fraction within the “preserved” range and in women [20,21]. Integrated analyses across PARADIGM-HF and PARAGON-HF suggest that treatment effect declines as ejection fraction rises, with the clearest extension of benefit into HFmrEF and lower-range HFpEF [22]. PARAGLIDE-HF, in patients with EF >40% after worsening heart failure, demonstrated a modestly greater NT-proBNP reduction versus valsartan [23], and the prespecified participant-level pooled PARAGLIDE-HF/PARAGON-HF analysis suggested fewer worsening heart-failure events, particularly at EF below normal [24]. Renal analyses in PARAGON-HF suggested slower eGFR decline and fewer adverse renal outcomes with sacubitril/valsartan than valsartan [25].

Current practice therefore places sacubitril/valsartan as foundational therapy for symptomatic chronic HFrEF, preferably replacing ACEI/ARB once blood pressure, renal function, potassium, and angioedema history are reviewed [26]. The 2022 AHA/ACC/HFSA guideline gives ARNI a central role in HFrEF and weaker, selected-use recommendations in HFmrEF/HFpEF [27]. ESC guidance similarly prioritizes ARNI among HFrEF disease-modifying therapies [28], with the 2023 update emphasizing rapid implementation of foundational therapy after diagnosis or hospitalization [29]. Future work should define optimal sequencing with sodium–glucose cotransporter-2 inhibitors, mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists, and device therapy; clarify benefit in lower-range HFpEF phenotypes; and improve initiation in populations underrepresented in trials. PIONEER-HF’s design illustrates the modern paradigm: move evidence-based therapy earlier, during vulnerable transitions, while individualizing titration to congestion, systolic pressure, kidney function, and patient goals [30].
